hints.junior: Any env var starting with REACT_APP_, VITE_, or NEXT_PUBLIC_ is in your JavaScript bundle. Open DevTools Sources and search; you can find it in seconds.
hints.mid: Minification is not security. Any determined person (or bot scanner) can extract a key from a minified bundle in under a minute.
hints.staff: Gitleaks and GitHub secret scanning catch keys in git history. A key that was ever committed (even if removed) should be rotated. Git history is permanent.

hints.junior: The broken demo has a fake API key in the bundle. Search for 'KEY' in DevTools Sources: you'll find it. The fixed version makes the same call through /api/proxy.
hints.mid: Check the Network tab request URLs. Broken: key is a URL parameter (visible in logs, proxies, CDNs). Fixed: URL is /api/proxy, key is on the server.
hints.staff: Run strings on the production bundle to verify no key leaked. This is a good addition to your deployment CI checklist.

hints.junior: Three patterns keep a key off the client entirely: a simple API proxy on your own backend, a single serverless function, or a thin BFF server. Pick based on what you already have running, not which sounds fanciest.
hints.mid: The first line of defense is naming, not code: an env var without a public prefix like NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_ never enters the bundle at all — server-only by convention, before any proxy pattern even comes into play.
hints.staff: Treat any key that ever touched git history as permanently compromised, reverted commit or not. Git history doesn't forget, and rotation is the only real remediation once a key has been committed.

hints.junior: Run strings on your production bundle and search for your key's prefix before you ship — it takes seconds, and it's the same check an attacker would run first.
hints.mid: source-map-explorer and @next/bundle-analyzer both give you a treemap of exactly what shipped in your bundle. Run one before assuming minification hid anything.
hints.staff: Your proxy endpoint is still a public surface even with the key safely server-side — rate-limit it per-user or per-IP, and scope the underlying key itself (a Stripe restricted key with only the permissions your server actually needs, not full account access).

anecdotes.junior: A freelance client got a $3,000 AWS bill from a key they put in a React app. The key was scraped within hours of deployment. Key rotation + proxy fixed it.
anecdotes.mid: The pattern I see most often: team uses NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix 'because it needs to work on the client.' The fix: add a Next.js API route as a proxy, 10 minutes of work.
anecdotes.staff: Secret scanning bots are automated. GitHub Actions, npm publish, and Vercel deployments are all monitored by scanners looking for leaked API keys. Assume anything public is scanned.

sections.junior: Hey! Today we're fixing a security mistake that costs real money: putting API keys in frontend JavaScript where anyone can read them.
sections.mid: This case covers the secrets-in-bundle vulnerability: why client-side JavaScript is public, the proxy pattern, and serverless functions as a lightweight fix.
sections.staff: We're covering OWASP A02 cryptographic failures, the full secret management lifecycle (rotation, CI scanning, rate limiting), and framework-specific patterns for keeping secrets server-side.

sections.junior: Route the request through your own backend instead: your frontend calls your server, and your server is the one that holds the real key and calls the third-party API.
sections.mid: For a static site with no backend, a small serverless function works the same way, a Vercel or Netlify or Cloudflare function holds the key, and your frontend just calls that function's URL.
sections.staff: Beyond the proxy pattern itself: rotate any key that's ever leaked, rate-limit your proxy endpoint, and allowlist the third-party API to your server's IP rather than trusting client IPs.

sections.junior: Any environment variable with a public prefix, like REACT_APP or VITE or NEXT_PUBLIC, ends up baked straight into your JavaScript. Never put a real secret in one.
sections.mid: The proxy pattern is the actual fix: your frontend calls your backend, your backend calls the third-party API with the key, and the key never touches the client.
sections.staff: Add secret scanning to your CI pipeline to catch keys before they ship. Treat anything that was ever committed or bundled as permanently compromised and rotate it immediately.
